summary: Specifies how DNS software should handle resource record types it does not understand, so that new types no longer need changes to name server software. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: If a mail clerk meets a package type they do not know, they should just pass it on. This memo tells DNS servers to treat new record types that way.

subtitle: How DNS software should store and pass along record types it does not recognize, so new types need no server upgrades.

tldr.problem: Adding a new resource record type to DNS meant changing name server software on the authoritative server, the client, every slave server and sometimes caches and forwarders, so deployment was slow and expensive.
tldr.mechanism: Servers and resolvers must treat the data of an unknown record type as opaque binary and store and send it unchanged. The RFC also bans name compression inside new types and defines a generic text form for such records.
tldr.outcome: New record types can be deployed without touching intermediate servers. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by several later RFCs.

today: RFC 3597 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 4033, RFC 4034, RFC 4035, RFC 5395, RFC 6195 and RFC 6895, so read it together with those. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem With New Record Types
sections.content:
The DNS is built to be extended with new resource record (RR) types. In practice, introducing one required changes to name server software at the authoritative server that provides the data and at the client that uses it. It also required changes at all slave servers for the zone, and in some cases at the caching name servers and forwarders the client relies on.

The RFC says that because new server software is slow and expensive to deploy, the potential of the DNS for new services has never been fully realized. It proposes changes to name servers and to the way new RR types are defined so that future types are simpler to deploy.
sections.eli5: Every time someone invented a new kind of DNS record, all the helpers along the way had to be taught about it first. That took forever, so this memo teaches them to pass along things they do not understand.

sections.title: Unknown Types and Transparent Handling
sections.content:
An RR of unknown type is one whose RDATA format the DNS implementation does not know, and whose type is not an assigned QTYPE or Meta-TYPE as defined in RFC 2929. Such a record cannot be converted to a type-specific text format, compressed, or otherwise handled in a type-specific way. If the format depends on the class, the record is unknown when the format for that type and class combination is not known.

Name servers and resolvers MUST handle these records transparently: they treat the RDATA as unstructured binary data and store and transmit it without change. To keep equality comparison and the DNSSEC canonical form correct when a type is known to some servers but not others, servers MUST also preserve the RDATA of known types exactly, apart from compression changes the RFC allows. In particular, the character case of domain names that are not subject to compression MUST be preserved.
sections.eli5: When a server sees a record it does not understand, it should treat the contents like a sealed envelope. It keeps the envelope exactly as it is and hands it on without peeking or changing anything.

sections.title: No Compression Inside New Types
sections.content:
DNS messages can shorten domain names with compression pointers, but those pointers only make sense inside the message they came from. If a server copied RDATA containing a pointer into a new message, the pointer would refer to unrelated data and the name would be corrupted. So records with compression pointers in their RDATA cannot be handled transparently.

Servers MUST NOT compress domain names embedded in the RDATA of types that are class-specific or not well-known. The RFC defines well-known to mean only the RR types defined in RFC 1035. Because of this, the RFC updates RFC 2163 (which allowed compression in the PX record) and RFC 2535 (which allowed it in SIG and NXT records).

Receiving servers MUST decompress names in well-known types, and SHOULD also decompress RP, AFSDB, RT, SIG, PX, NXT, NAPTR and SRV. Future specifications for new types with domain names in their RDATA MUST NOT allow compression, and SHOULD say so explicitly. The owner name of a record is always eligible for compression.
sections.eli5: Compression is like writing "see page 3" instead of repeating a long address. That works in one letter but breaks if you copy the line into a different letter, so new record types are not allowed to use it.

sections.title: The Generic Text Format
sections.content:
In a master file, an unknown type is written as the word TYPE followed immediately by the decimal type number, and an unknown class as CLASS followed by the decimal class number. This keeps types, classes and TTL values distinguishable so both orderings of the RFC 1035 line format can still be parsed.

The RDATA of an unknown type is written as the token \#, then the RDATA length in octets as an unsigned decimal integer, then zero or more words of hexadecimal data, each with an even number of digits. Empty RDATA is written as just \# 0.

An implementation MAY also use this generic form for records of known type, which makes the resulting master file portable to servers that do not know them. Even then, all further processing MUST treat the record as a known type and apply its type-specific rules.
sections.eli5: This gives a plain way to write any record as a number plus a string of hex digits, a bit like writing a secret message as numbers. Any program can read it even without knowing what the message means.

sections.title: Equality, DNSSEC and Additional Sections
sections.content:
Protocols such as Dynamic Update (RFC 2136) compare records for equality. Two records of the same unknown type are equal when their RDATA is bitwise equal, and specifications for new types MUST NOT define type-specific comparison rules. As a result, embedded domain names are compared case-sensitively, so records that differ only in the case of an embedded name can coexist, much like TXT records that differ only in case.

DNSSEC lower-cases domain names embedded in RDATA in its canonical form, but that needs knowledge of where the names are, so it cannot be applied to unknown types. The canonical form stays unchanged for all RR types first published as RFCs before RFC 3597, and the RFC lists them: NS, MD, MF, CNAME, SOA, MB, MG, MR, PTR, HINFO, MINFO, MX, RP, AFSDB, RT, SIG, PX, NXT, NAPTR, KX, SRV, DNAME and A6. For all other types, no lower-casing of embedded names takes place. The owner name is always lower-cased.

Unknown types cause no additional section processing. Future types may define it, but it MUST be optional, since only servers that know the type can perform it.
sections.eli5: Two sealed envelopes count as the same only if every letter inside matches exactly, capitals included. That way every server reaches the same answer, whether or not it knows what is in the envelope.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The RFC states that the specification is not believed to cause any new security problems, nor to solve any existing ones. It also asks IANA to do nothing.

The security-relevant detail is in the DNSSEC rules covered above: the canonical form used for signatures depends on whether embedded names are lower-cased, which is why the RFC fixes it per record type rather than leaving it to what each server happens to know.
sections.eli5: The authors say this change does not make DNS safer or less safe. They only made sure everyone checks the signatures in exactly the same way.
